result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.adamic_adar_index()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute Adamic-Adar index for node pairs. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L16399-L16506){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.adamic_adar_index(ebunch=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Adamic-Adar index](/assets/graphs/adamic-adar-index.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Nodes B and E are outlined in the accent color with their shared neighbors C and D filled in accent; badges give C degree 3 and D degree 2. The card sums 1 over the log of each degree, 0.910 + 1.443, for an Adamic-Adar index of 2.353." width="100%"} For each pair of nodes `(u, v)`, computes `Σ(1 / log(|N(w)|))` for all common neighbors `w`. This gives more weight to common neighbors that themselves have fewer connections (rarer connections are more significant). The logarithm is the natural log, so a shared neighbor of degree 2 contributes about `1.44`, one of degree 3 about `0.91`, and a hub of degree 100 only about `0.22`. The graph is not modified. Adamic-Adar is one of the most reliable local link-prediction scores and is useful for: - recommending connections where sharing a niche contact means more than sharing a celebrity contact - ranking candidate links in social, collaboration, or biological networks - comparing against `common_neighbors()` (no degree penalty) and `resource_allocation_index()` (a stronger penalty) The measure is intended for undirected graphs. On a directed graph, neighbors and degrees are taken from *outgoing* edges, and a shared neighbor with out-degree `0` or `1` contributes nothing (its logarithm would be zero or undefined). When `ebunch=` is `None`, every pair of non-adjacent nodes is scored, which is quadratic in the number of nodes; pass `ebunch=` on large graphs. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ebunch]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[tuple[Union[int, str], Union[int, str]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : List of `(u, v)` node pairs to score. Each node can be given as a node ID (`int`) or label (`str`). Pairs are scored even if `u` and `v` are already connected, and they are returned in the order given. If `None` (the default), all pairs of nodes that are not already connected (in either direction) are scored, each unordered pair once, in no particular order. A node that doesn't exist raises a `ValueError`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int, float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of `(u, v, index)` tuples where index is the Adamic-Adar score (`0.0` when the nodes share no neighbors). Nodes are reported as node IDs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a node in `ebunch=` does not exist in the graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Adamic-Adar index refines common-neighbor counting by weighting each shared neighbor $w$ by $\dfrac{1}{\log |N(w)|}$: $\mathrm{AA}(u, v) = \sum_{w \in N(u) \cap N(v)} \dfrac{1}{\log |N(w)|}$. The intuition, borrowed from information theory, is that rare neighbors carry more evidence of a real connection than popular hubs everyone touches. The score is unbounded above and empirically beats plain common-neighbor counting on many real networks. Runs in $O(k)$ per pair. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Nodes `2` and `3` share the hub (node `1`) as their only common neighbor. Because the hub has degree 8, its contribution is `1 / ln(8)`, about `0.48`, well below the count of 1 that `common_neighbors()` would give: ::: {#cb487ea7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_node() # hub, node 1 for i in range(2, 10): graph.add_node() graph.add_edge(1, i) # hub connected to all others graph.adamic_adar_index([(2, 3)]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [(2, 3, 0.48089834696298783)] ``` ::: ::: The weighting can reorder candidates. Below, `Ann` and `Bob` share one low-degree contact (`Kim`, degree 2), while `Cat` and `Dan` share two well-connected hubs. Common neighbors ranks `Cat`/`Dan` first (2 vs. 1); Adamic-Adar ranks `Ann`/`Bob` first because the hubs are discounted: ::: {#cb387960 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_nodes(["Ann", "Bob", "Kim", "Cat", "Dan", "H1", "H2"]) graph.add_nodes([f"x{i}" for i in range(12)]) graph.add_edge("Ann", "Kim").add_edge("Bob", "Kim") for hub in ["H1", "H2"]: graph.add_edge("Cat", hub).add_edge("Dan", hub) for i in range(6): graph.add_edge(hub, f"x{i}" if hub == "H1" else f"x{i + 6}") pairs = [("Ann", "Bob"), ("Cat", "Dan")] [ (cn[2], round(aa[2], 3)) for cn, aa in zip(graph.common_neighbors(pairs), graph.adamic_adar_index(pairs)) ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [(1, 1.443), (2, 0.962)] ``` ::: :::
